title: The Megaphone, Leased
prompt: The Onion just leased Alex Jones's megaphone for $81,000 a month — from a receiver, not from Jones. Is that a debt being collected, or a court renting out one man's transmitter to his loudest mocker?
framing: On April 20, 2026, The Onion's parent company, Global Tetrahedron, said it had signed a deal with Gregory Milligan — the receiver a Travis County judge put over Alex Jones's assets on August 13, 2025 — to license the Infowars name, domains and intellectual property for six months at $81,000 a month, with an option to renew. A judge still has to approve it. It is not a purchase. The Onion's purchase, announced as the winning bid at the federal bankruptcy auction on November 14, 2024, was thrown out on December 10, 2024, when Judge Christopher Lopez found the sealed-bid process lacked transparency and left money on the table; a rival bid tied to Jones offered $3.5 million in cash against The Onion's $1.75 million. The Connecticut families who won a $1.3 billion defamation judgment over Jones's Sandy Hook lies are creditors of the receivership, not the counterparty to this deal. Tim Heidecker is named creative director. Ben Collins, The Onion's CEO, says that eight years after the parents sued, they will get 'some justice, and even some money,' and that merchandise proceeds will reach them. Jones is on the air.

meta.source: Slot: evergreen free-speech / satire-vs-accountability archetype. Sources: CNN 2026-04-20; Rolling Stone (Texas appeals court pauses takeover, May 28 hearing); Hollywood Reporter (Heidecker + Ben Collins); TIME 2026-04-28. Why: bilateral free-speech inversion + Heidecker satire/sincerity collapse as a denomination test.

header.title: The Onion wins Infowars at auction / the free-speech inversion
header.prompt: The Onion wins Alex Jones's Infowars at auction to repay the Sandy Hook families.
header.framing: The Onion won Alex Jones's Infowars at auction, paying the Sandy Hook families he defamed, and will parody him on his own platform. Accountability — or using the courts to seize a megaphone?

fluid.text: He defamed grieving families and lost in court. The law is just collecting.

coalition.text: I wanted him held to account — but 'seize his platform' is a new power.

denominated.text: Hand the fascist's megaphone to the people he tormented. Good.

fluid.text: The verdict's fair — but courts handing a platform to his enemies should scare us.

coalition.text: We warned about lawfare for years; now we're quiet because we hate the guy.

denominated.text: They couldn't beat Infowars in the market, so they seized it in court.

fluid.text: No censor did this — the people he lied about turned his platform into a joke.

coalition.text: I'm cheering — but is this justice, or just taking his megaphone?

denominated.text: Drag him. The clown who mocked dead kids has to wear our jokes now.

fluid.text: He lied, yes — but a billion-dollar verdict erasing a dissident is annihilation.

coalition.text: Deplatforming is deplatforming, even when my side makes him a martyr.

denominated.text: A kangaroo court executed Infowars and handed the scalp to globalist comedians.

LF.text: The accountability left is holding the legitimate object — a serial defamer was found liable and the law is collecting — while keeping sight of how unusual it is for a court process to end with a media platform in his opponents' hands.

LC.text: The accountability left is starting to notice its own slide from 'pay the families' to 'seize the megaphone,' and only the people still inside the cheer can feel the moment justice turned into appetite.

LD.text: The accountability left reads the seizure as pure victory — the fascist's platform handed to decent people — and treats any worry about precedent as sympathy for a man who lied about murdered children.

RF.text: The principled right is holding the free-speech line it always claimed — that litigating an outlet into your opponents' hands is a weapon that won't stay aimed one way — without pretending Jones earned anything but the judgment against him.

RC.text: The principled right is watching its own anti-deplatforming creed go quiet because the target is someone it hates, and noticing that a principle invoked only for allies was never a principle.

RD.text: The right is performing persecution: a defamation judgment becomes 'lawfare,' a bankruptcy auction becomes 'execution,' and the man who monetized Sandy Hook becomes a free-speech martyr.

zFirstAuthoring.authorNote: The draft was wrong on its premise, not its date. April 20, 2026 is a real object — but it is a six-month, $81,000-a-month LICENSE from a Travis County state receiver, not a purchase; the 2024 auction win was voided December 10, 2024; the families are creditors of the estate, not the sellers. Hardest call: whether the object had finished forming, since the license needed a judge and never got one cleanly; I set the window at the signed instrument and pushed approval, the April 29 appellate pause, the Texas Supreme Court and the July 2 relaunch into afterWindow. z surprised me at B.fluid: the only genuinely positive right-side reading of a seizure is the driest one. Least sure rim: A.denominated at −0.2. Soft dates: the license signing vs announcement; the day the bankruptcy judge ceded to Travis County (placed 2026-05-15).
zFirstAuthoring.rulings: stations stand as authored (Sailor 09-21: ship, then read on the surface)

z.pos: The transfer actually lands: a judge signs, the receiver hands over the domains, the name and the archive, the $81,000 a month and the sale of what's left move real money toward the Sandy Hook families, and the thing Jones built stops being his.
z.neg: Nothing moves. It is a signed paper inside a receivership that appeals can stall indefinitely; the rent funds administrators, the families get a line item, and Jones keeps broadcasting under whatever name he likes.

fluid.text: This is what a judgment looks like when it finally has teeth. Milligan has had authority over Jones's assets since August 13, 2025, and $81,000 a month is real money moving into an estate the Connecticut families have a claim on. Six months with a renewal option is a modest, reversible step, and it is exactly the kind of thing a judge should approve.
fluid.zReason: Receivership law does move assets; a named receiver plus a signed instrument plus a monthly number is how collection actually works, and this voice has watched it work before.

coalition.text: I want the families paid and I am uneasy about how this reads. A court renting a broadcaster's name to a comedy company is defensible as asset management and indefensible as a headline, and Jones will run on that headline for a year. Approve it — and stop calling it justice. The judgment is $1.3 billion. This is $486,000 over six months.
coalition.zReason: Holds the mechanism as sound and the arithmetic as devastating — belief in delivery survives the legal question and dies on the size of the number.

denominated.text: The receiver holds it. The families hold a number on paper. Those are not the same thing and never have been.
denominated.zReason: At the rim the object is gone and only the holder is left; this voice has seen enough estates to know who gets paid first, and it is not the plaintiffs.

fluid.text: Strip the names off it. A defendant with a $1.3 billion judgment against him did not pay, a Travis County judge appointed a receiver on August 13, 2025, and the receiver is renting an intangible asset for $81,000 a month. That is black-letter collection practice. If we want receiverships to work when we are the creditor, they work here too.
fluid.zReason: Believes the machinery delivers because the machinery is ordinary — this is the least exotic thing a receiver does, and the exotic part is only whose name is on the asset.

instrument.holder: Texas collection law, executed by the receiver

coalition.text: Two things. Lopez was right on December 10, 2024 that a sealed-bid process taking $1.75 million over $3.5 million was not maximizing value. And now the same assets are being leased, not sold, to the same bidder. I can defend the receivership and still ask why this estate keeps choosing the lower number.
coalition.zReason: The process is legitimate and the pattern is not; belief in delivery falls because the estate has twice preferred the buyer it likes to the bid that pays more.

denominated.text: A single Travis County district court now decides who gets to be Infowars. That is the whole story, and it is not a story about money.
denominated.zReason: At the rim the object has become a jurisdiction; nothing this voice believes about that court suggests it delivers to anyone it recognizes.

fluid.text: Eight years since those parents sued, and what arrived is a lease. Collins says merch money gets back to the families and I believe he means it. But $81,000 a month goes to a receiver, and I have never once seen a receivership hand a working family the check on the front page.
fluid.zReason: Engaged with the instrument and unwilling to pretend rent is recovery; the doubt is about routing, not about good faith.

coalition.text: I want Jones off the air and I do not want his archive turned into a bit. Both. Those families were hunted for years by people who believed him, and the answer on the table is a six-month rental with a renewal option and a creative director. That is not nothing. It is also not what was owed.
coalition.zReason: Holds two incompatible wants and finds the instrument delivers neither — not silence, not payment, only a format.

denominated.text: A media company rented it. The parents got a line item. Same as always.
denominated.zReason: The rim does not argue; it reports a pattern. Ownership changed hands among companies and the people the harm happened to were a creditor class.

fluid.text: They could not buy it in 2024 so now they are leasing it — $81,000 a month for a name and a mailing list. A judge picked a man on August 13, 2025 to hold Alex Jones's keys, and that man is renting his voice to the people who make a living mocking him. Call it whatever you want. He is on the air tonight, and that is the part that matters.
fluid.zReason: Believes the paper is real enough to fear and useless to him; the delivery he cares about is the broadcast continuing, and that has nothing to do with the license.

instrument.holder: the receiver, acting for the plaintiffs

coalition.text: He said things about dead children that were false and he should pay every dollar. And a court should not be in the business of renting a man's transmitter to his opponents. I can hold both, and I think the second one outlives the first by thirty years.
coalition.zReason: Concedes the debt entirely and still expects nothing good from the instrument, because the precedent is the deliverable and the precedent runs against him.

denominated.text: They own the words now. That is it. That is the ruling.
denominated.zReason: Lowest z in the set and the rim earns it: there is no version of a court-appointed stranger with the keys that this voice reads as delivering anything to him, ever.

instrument.holder: the courts and the media companies they favor

LF.text: The left reads the April 20, 2026 license as collection law finally biting: a receiver with authority since August 13, 2025 renting an asset for $81,000 a month into an estate the Sandy Hook families can claim against.

LC.text: The left holds two things at once — that the receivership is legitimate and that $486,000 over six months is not what a $1.3 billion judgment was supposed to mean.

LD.text: At the rim the left stops arguing and names a holder: a media company rented it, the parents got a line item.

RF.text: The right reads it, at its most institutional, as unremarkable Texas practice — a debtor who did not pay, a receiver appointed on August 13, 2025, an intangible asset put to rent.

RC.text: The right concedes the lie about dead children and still refuses the remedy, arguing a court renting a man's transmitter to his opponents will outlive the debt it was meant to settle.

RD.text: At the rim the right stops arguing too and reduces the whole thing to custody: they own the words now.

window.why: The object finished forming in one day: on April 20, 2026 The Onion's parent, Global Tetrahedron, announced a signed six-month license of the Infowars name, domains and IP from court-appointed receiver Gregory Milligan at $81,000 a month. The signed instrument is the object; judicial approval and the appellate fight that followed are after the window.

antiValentRationale: [B.fluid] A right-institutional voice underwriting the seizure of a right-wing broadcaster's brand, on pure collection-law grounds, against its own station's reflex.

objectLayer.stated: A signed six-month license, at $81,000 a month with a renewal option, of the Infowars name, domains and intellectual property from court-appointed receiver Gregory Milligan to The Onion's parent company, Global Tetrahedron, pending judicial approval.
objectLayer.operative: A state receivership monetizing a judgment debtor's brand by renting it to his loudest mocker, while the debtor keeps his microphone, his audience and his appeals.
objectLayer.inversion: Sold as the Sandy Hook families finally collecting, it is the families' court-appointed agent collecting rent. The money enters an estate rather than their hands, the instrument is a lease rather than a transfer, and nothing in it stops Alex Jones from talking.

split.seam: the receiver — whether a court-appointed stranger holding the keys is collection working or collection replacing the thing collected
split.rationale: Inside the window the argument is not left-versus-right about Jones; almost nobody defends what he said. It is institutional-versus-populist about the instrument. The centers of all four stations engage the license on its terms — price, term, approval, what a receiver may lawfully rent. As the radius grows the object thins to a holder question, and by the rim every station has stopped arguing and simply named whose hands it is in. The peel is clean because the license is genuinely unfinished on April 20, 2026: it needs a judge, so belief in delivery does all the work.

zPattern.note: Every rim signs negative and every rim's instrument.trusted is false, including A's. The rim is where holder-trust collapses regardless of station: left-institutional ends at 'the estate holds it,' right-populist at 'they own the words.' The centers are where the spread lives — A and B both positive, C and D both negative — which is why the scalar runs along y and not x.
